summary: Defines OSPF extensions that let a Path Computation Client automatically find Path Computation Elements and learn what they can do. This helps when the PCE participates in the IGP. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5088 lets OSPF advertise which routers or servers can compute network paths. The advertisements tell clients where a path-computation service is and what kinds of paths it can handle.

subtitle: How OSPF advertises path-computation services and their capabilities to routers in a domain.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Client needs to discover Path Computation Elements and learn enough about their capabilities to choose a service.
tldr.mechanism: A PCE advertises a PCE Discovery TLV in an OSPF Router Information LSA. The TLV carries its address, path scope, domains, preferences, and capability flags.
tldr.outcome: OSPF flooding informs clients about PCEs that appear, fail, or change. PCE selection itself and discovery across autonomous-system boundaries are outside this RFC. RFC 5088 is updated by RFC 9353.

today: RFC 5088 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008 and is updated by RFC 9353.

sections.title: Discovering Path Computation Elements
sections.content:
A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) to calculate a network path. A network may have multiple PCEs with different capabilities, so clients need to discover them and notice changes or failures.

RFC 5088 defines this discovery for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. A PCE advertises information through the OSPF Router Information LSA, which is flooded through an area or routing domain. The RFC does not define how a client chooses among the PCEs it discovers.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can learn which PCEs are available by receiving OSPF advertisements. This RFC defines the information those advertisements carry.

sections.title: What a PCE Advertises
sections.content:
The discovery information identifies a PCE's IPv4 or IPv6 address, the path scopes it can compute, the domains it can see, neighboring domains it can compute toward, and its capabilities. The scope can include intra-area, inter-area, inter-AS, or inter-layer path computation.

The PCE chooses whether its advertisement is flooded within selected OSPF areas or across the full OSPF routing domain. Information is expected to be relatively stable, changing when configuration, activation, deactivation, or failure changes the PCE's state.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE advertises where it can be reached and which path calculations it supports. Its advertisement can be limited to selected OSPF areas or shared across the routing domain.

sections.title: The PCED TLV and Its Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The PCE Discovery TLV, or PCED TLV, has type 6 and contains an unordered set of sub-TLVs. It uses a two-octet type, a two-octet length, and a value, with padding to four-octet alignment. It is carried in an OSPF Router Information LSA.

The PCE-ADDRESS and PATH-SCOPE sub-TLVs are required. PCE-DOMAIN, NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN, and PCE-CAP-FLAGS are optional. An unrecognized sub-TLV is silently ignored; a malformed PCED TLV is handled as a malformed LSA under normal OSPF procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCED TLV is a labeled container inside an OSPF advertisement. It must include an address and path scope; the other fields add domain and capability details.

sections.title: Path Scope and PCE Preference
sections.content:
The PATH-SCOPE sub-TLV indicates which path scopes the PCE supports. Its flags cover intra-area, inter-area, inter-AS, and inter-layer computation, as well as default-PCE roles. Four three-bit preference fields rank the PCE for the corresponding scopes; a value of 7 is the highest preference.

A client or network policy decides how to use the preference values, including for weighted load balancing. The capability flags can announce features such as bidirectional or diverse path computation and request prioritization.
sections.plainLanguage: The path-scope field lists the kinds of paths a PCE can calculate. Preference values help local policy rank PCEs for each kind of request.

sections.title: Flooding, Changes, and Security
sections.content:
A PCE's advertisement must be withdrawn or updated when the PCE is deactivated or its state changes. A change to PCED information must not trigger an OSPF shortest-path-first computation. A router that does not support the PCED TLV silently ignores it.

Discovery relies on OSPF security within the administrative domain. OSPF mechanisms can protect LSA authenticity and integrity, but OSPF does not encrypt LSAs. The RFC also requires controls that limit how frequently PCE information changes and how often clients process changes or switch PCEs. RFC 5088 is updated by RFC 9353.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF advertisements must reflect changes to a PCE, but changing them does not require routers to recalculate routes. Authentication can protect the information, but the advertisements are not encrypted.

items.label: PCE-ADDRESS
items.desc: Address used to reach the PCE.

items.label: PCE-DOMAIN
items.desc: Domain where the PCE has visibility.

items.label: NEIG-PCE-DOMAIN
items.desc: Neighbor domain toward which the PCE can compute.
